Keywords: energy, GDP, economic Work, Money, productivity, Pierre Campergue,
World Bank, materiality of growth, decoupling, productive transformation
1
Introduction
Modern economic debates often treat growth as an abstract monetary or statistical
phenomenon. GDP increases, corporate margins rise, financial valuations expand,
and national accounts appear to describe the economy through flows of currency, ser-
vices, income, and expenditure. Yet production remains physically situated. Goods
must be extracted, transformed, transported, maintained, repaired, cleaned, assem-
bled, and powered. Even in service economies, the apparent immateriality of value
creation often rests on material processes displaced elsewhere in the supply chain.
Pierre Campergue’s corpus addresses this problem at the level of economic language.
His manuscript, Reflections on the Economic Power of Work and the Mechanical
Power of Money, does not simply claim that economics is thermodynamics. Such a
reduction would misrepresent the project. Campergue’s effort is primarily semantic,
analytical, and formal: he seeks to define economic variables precisely, distinguish
supports from values, distinguish labour from economic Work, and distinguish flows
from transformations.
This empirical note does not attempt to prove the full corpus.
Its purpose is nar-
rower. It asks whether publicly available macroeconomic data provide evidence for a
persistent coupling between real GDP and energy use. This question matters because
Campergue’s framework gives central importance to productive transformation and
to the work required to alter productive conditions. If economic growth were fully
decoupled from energy at the world scale, one important macroeconomic intuition
of the corpus would be weakened. If, however, world GDP and energy use remain
strongly associated, the empirical result supports the view that growth remains ma-
terially conditioned, even when this condition is obscured by accounting aggregates
and territorial boundaries.
The note therefore treats the code in this repository as an empirical appendix to the
corpus, not as a proof of the entire theoretical construction.
2
Conceptual background: Campergue’s corpus
Campergue’s manuscript is organized around a set of distinctions that ordinary eco-
nomic language often blurs.
The first distinction is between Cash and Money. Cash is the monetary support: the
unit, sign, inscription, or circulating medium. Money, in Campergue’s terminology,
refers to the economic value or purchasing power carried by that support. This dis-
tinction prevents the creation or movement of monetary units from being confused
with the creation of real purchasing power.

wish to spend a night at the Pic du Midi de Bigorre, acquire a pedigree
puppy, personalise his vehicle, have lunch in a starred restaurant, visit
catacombs, reserve a place for a lunar or marsian trip, etc. However, to
achieve each of these hypotheses, the person will always be subject to
constraints which may be of various kinds, as already mentioned above.
What has just been exposed for the physical field applies in a similar way
in the economic field. Indeed :
depending on the Product, the pecuniary constraint can be
very variable. It is much lower to acquire a low-range flat
than a rich villa,
depending on the agent, the constraint also varies
significantly. It is much higher for a person on minimum
social benefits than for a major shareholder in a large
multinational company.
Moreover, it's clear that the higher the constraints, the less choice can be
made and vice versa. If the constraints were zero, anyone would be able to
make all their choices without restriction. Thus, from an economic point of
view, the more Money an individual has at his disposal, the more he will be
able to satisfy his choice and conversely, which is perfectly banal.
In order to enrich a society, the goal is that as many of its members as
possible be in a position to fill their acquisition opportunities. For this it's
therefore necessary to reduce the constraints weighing on these agents. But
this procedure is absolutely independent of the consumer's choice and
therefore of the consumer. Whatever the consumer's desires and wishes,
the only useful action is to ensure that he can satisfy them and therefore
has additional financial capacity. In any economic society, individuals have
more or less financial possibilities (Money). In order to enable as many of
them as possible to acquire goods and services, it's imperative that their
prices are as low as possible. Indeed, if prices decrease the financial
constraint falls by as much and the individual can make his choice more
easily.
This essay therefore seeks to understand by which mechanisms and
phenomena it's possible to reduce the financial constraints restricting the
realisation of individuals' choices. It is the procedure and methodology for
reducing constraints, and therefore prices, that this study proposes to know
and master, while abandoning that of choice in the strict sense of the term.
